title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1LC0RD_---1LD_1RB1RE_1LA0LB_0LA0LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1LC0RD_---1LD_1RB1RE_1LA0LB_0LA0LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The macro words and the transfer phase are identified, and Lean proves the sweeps over (10)^n; the rule for a whole round is not known yet.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (C0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 43,573 cells have been visited and 16,600 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.107). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.525).

claims.title: The sweeps
claims.text: Six shift rules: B, D and E run right and A and F run left over (10)^n or (01)^n, for all n and any tapes around (one copy by rfl, all copies by TM.cross_r / TM.cross_l).

claims.title: Round starts to 5·10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: A C run to 5·109 steps, sampled at each left-end extension: the tape is a list of counters a^x 1^(6k) (a = 10) followed by one long block of ones that grows by about 4/3 per round (8,750, 22,510, 29,966, 39,758, 52,630, 97,478 …).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known; no round rule has been found yet, so the question is not reduced to a map.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RC_1LC1RF_1RE0LD_1LC1LA_---1RD_0RB0RA up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine keeps one long block at its right end that grows about 4/3 per round, re-encoded each time, and a list of counters on the left. Its round rule has not been found yet.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 43,573 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: One growing block and a list of counters
html: Write a for 10 and c for 100. The right end of the tape holds one long block that changes its encoding from round to round: a run of ones, then copies of c, then copies of a. In the main phase the head zigzags between the right end and the front of a c-block, turning one c into two a at the right end each trip; the tape grows there by one cell per trip (the square-root side).

Between these phases the head works through a list of counters on the left, runs of a separated by runs of ones whose lengths are multiples of 6; only then does the tape grow on the left (the logarithmic side). The long block grows by about 4/3 per round, like the related machine 1RB1LF_1LC0RD_---1LA_0LA0RE_1LA1RA_1LB0LD, but here the counters on the left grow as well.
The machine halts only on C reading 0, which needs B on a 0 with a 0 to its left. No rule for a whole round is known yet, so whether that ever happens is open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.107). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.525).
After 109 steps the tape spans 43,573 cells (239 left of the start, 30,040 right), with a density of 1s of 0.381.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: One long block grows about 4/3 per round while being re-encoded (ones, 100s, 10s), with a list of counters on the left; the round rule is not yet known.
